passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Urbanization and Internal Migration

A Urbanization concentrates population and economic activity in cities, transforming land use, labour markets, and social networks across nations at uneven speeds. Internal migration from rural hinterlands to metropolitan cores supplies workers for services and manufacturing while draining remittance-dependent villages of young adults. Governments promote urban agglomeration for productivity gains linked to knowledge spillovers, yet congestion, housing costs, and pollution externalities challenge liveability rankings. Sociologists examine how hukou-style registration systems and informal settlements shape access to schools and clinics for newly arrived households seeking opportunity. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

B Push factors include agricultural mechanisation, climate shocks on rain-fed crops, and violence that makes countryside residence untenable. Pull factors feature higher expected wages, educational institutions, and anonymity that loosens traditional surveillance by kin. Migration theories distinguish permanent relocation from circular flows tied to harvest seasons or construction booms. Social capital theorists argue migrants leverage ethnic enclave ties to find housing and jobs, though exploitation by intermediaries charging illegal fees persists in corridors linking interior provinces to coastal factory zones with dormitory regimes. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

C Infrastructure investment in transit-oriented development aims to connect suburbs with employment centres, reducing commute times that erode family life. Megacity planners experiment with satellite towns to decentralise functions, yet employment lags can create bedroom communities without local jobs. Informal transport fills gaps where formal buses are unreliable, creating safety risks especially for women travelling at night. Smart city initiatives collect mobility data to optimise signals, raising privacy debates about surveillance normalised as efficiency upgrades welcomed by tech vendors pitching integrated platforms to mayors facing re-election cycles. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

D Housing markets strain under demand shocks when migration outpaces construction, inflating rents and crowding tenants into subdivided flats lacking fire exits. Rent control debates pit tenant protections against developer incentives, while public housing queues stretch for years. Gentrification displaces long-term residents as creative industries colonise formerly affordable districts, altering cultural character and triggering activism for community land trusts. The author notes that without inclusive zoning, urban growth rewards landowners while precarious migrants remain one paycheck from eviction in overheated speculative markets fueled by global capital seeking yield. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

E Social integration varies: second-generation urban-born children may assimilate linguistically while parents retain rural dialects, creating intergenerational negotiation at home. Discrimination in hiring against regional accents or surnames associated with migrant status perpetuates occupational segregation into hazardous informal work. Community organisations offer legal aid on contracts and occupational safety, yet outreach struggles when populations are highly mobile. Religious and festival networks reproduce village solidarity in urban parishes, buffering anomie theorists associate with dense anonymous environments where traditional moral controls weaken. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

F Governance challenges include updating master plans participatory enough to incorporate migrant voices often excluded from neighbourhood councils. Census undercounts undocumented movers, skewing fiscal transfers that fund schools in receiving districts. Pandemic lockdowns exposed dependence on migrant delivery workers while denying them residence permits in some cities they served. Climate adaptation plans must anticipate inland destinations as coastal megacities face sea-level rise, potentially redirecting flows toward secondary cities requiring proactive investment in water and employment rather than reactive shantytown clearance campaigns repeating historical errors. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

G Looking ahead, the author believes equitable urbanization demands land and labour policies acknowledging migrants as permanent contributors, not temporary inputs. Regional development should reduce coerced migration driven by destitution. If cities brand themselves as global hubs while neglecting affordable housing, social friction will intensify. Balanced strategies combining rural livelihood support, inclusive urban services, and accountable planning offer a more stable trajectory than either forced rural retention or unchecked speculative growth that treats shelter as financial asset first and human right second. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.
